Corsair Chiplet: Built Using Modular Hardware Blocks

  • Corsair SOC Chiplet
    • 4 Quads
    • Global RISC V Control Core
    • LPDDR & PCIe Subsystems
    • D2D
  • Quad
    • Locus of control, RISC-V + DE
    • Ease of Programmability
    • 4 Slices clustered with a RISC V Control Core
    • Instruction Dispatcher (DE)
  • Slice
    • 2x Cores sharing a Global Memory (GM)
    • Data Reshaper, Low-Latency NOC

Compute: Energy Efficient DIMC Architecture

  • Logic-rule SRAM array in TSMC 6nm
  • Dual bit-serial, 4 bit-parallel MAC array
  • Supports 64x64 Matrix Ops in MXINT8
  • Supports 64x128 Matrix Ops in MXINT4
  • Fully digital design for accuracy and precision

Core Architecture: Shared Buffers and SIMD Unit

  • MX block floating point datatypes
  • DIMC array with high BW Stash SRAM
  • Inline partial product reduction
  • 4 wide VLIW Vector SIMD unit
  • On-the-fly quantization/format conversions

Memory System: Global Memory, Stash, and LPDDR

  • Stash (ST): Where weights and caches are stored
  • Global Memory (GM): Where activations are stored
  • Stash and Global memory:
    • Vector (64 bytes) addressable on-chip SRAM
    • DMA for contiguous and/or strided data with looping
    • Inline HW for transpose, tensor insertion and extraction
    • Inline HW for datatype conversions
  • LPDDR:
    • Two interfaces per chiplet: 51.2GB/s (aggregate)
    • Multiple model storage, Prefix caching, dormant KV cache

Interconnect: Network on Chip, Die-to-die, PCIe

  • Hierarchical all-to-all network-on-chip (NoC)
  • Extended to multiple chiplets, fully connected die-to-die (D2D)
  • Extended to multiple MCMs over PCIe
  • [Extended to multiple nodes over Ethernet]

Gang Control Cluster and ISA Graph Execution

  • Deferred last step of lowering
  • Causal ordering guarantee
  • No timing assumptions
  • No data or structural hazards
  • Precise unit behavior control per ISA op instance
  • Ability to target down to a single DIMC/SIMD/DMA/DRE unit

  • Deferred lowering allows JIT resolution of code sections
  • Tensor addresses from host: input, output, cache
  • Parameters of each iteration: query identity, sampling, batch size, temperature
  • Control paths: branches, conditional segments, loop counts
  • All without recompilation or rewriting of kernels

Aviator software stack

The first half showed the whole stack. This half covers the Model Builder SDK and its kernels, Core and Dist (I'll call them ES Core and ES Dist), the debug tools, and Aviator Fabric for scale-out.

The programmable unit: the gang

Each gang has its own program, memory and control.

32 gangs per card. Each is a processing element (PE).

On a GPU you write the logic of one thread, and every thread shares one address space. On Corsair the unit you program is the gang: its own program, its own SRAM, its own control. A gang's SRAM is its GM and its stash, plus small buffers in each core. No gang can load or store another's memory: data reaches another gang only as a message, a MOVE into its memory. That is why the next slide reaches for MPI.

There is a shared DDR off the chip, also reached only by moves. In the fast mode it doesn't hold the weights: those stay in each gang's stash, loaded once.

Inside the card, gangs act like MPI ranks

On a GPU you write a thread. Here you write a gang kernel.

MPI, as an analogyCorsair
a ranka gang, with its own program
the rank's memorythe gang's SRAM
each rank runs at its own paceso does each gang: no lockstep
send and receivea MOVE into the other gang's memory, then a DE_BARRIER on the receiver
collectivesin the library: broadcast, all-gather, reduce-scatter
launching the ranksenqueueing a job

Inside one card, the 32 gangs behave like the ranks of an MPI program: each runs its own program on its own data, at its own pace. One gang talks to another by writing into its memory with a MOVE; the receiver waits on a DE_BARRIER. Collectives are library modules.

This is an analogy inside the device only. On the host, MPI is real, and one rank drives one card; that comes later.

Column-parallel C = A × B on two gangs

The input A changes every call. B is loaded once and stays in the stash.

1Two gangs split N

2Inside gang 0 4 slices × 2 cores

A core has 8 DIMCs for the matmul, a SIMD engine, and its own input, weight and output buffers.

Our running example: a matmul split by columns over two gangs. A changes every call; B is loaded once and stays in the stash.

Each core runs two MATMULs. Its 8 DIMCs each take a 64-row tile of K, so one MATMUL covers 512 of K; the second accumulates.

Where every byte goes

Each arrow is one instruction. B goes to the stash once, at load.

Tensor classes

Each memory has its SDK object: DDRTensor, GMTensor, STTensor (red, above). The program on the next slide creates A and C as DDRTensors and places them in GM.

Wide sums, FP16 out

Partial sums stay wide (BFP32) in the output buffers. The OB2OB moves add them; the last add writes the total as FP16, and OB2GM carries it to GM unchanged.

The first half's MXINT8 is MB-SDK's BFP16_64: 8-bit values, one exponent per 64. (The OCP MX spec's MXINT8 uses blocks of 32.)

Every arrow is an instruction in the program. A arrives as block floating point; B was put in the stash once, at load.

Partial sums stay wide in the output buffers. The last add writes the total back as FP16, and the move to GM carries it unchanged. The adds are done by the moves themselves, not by a separate instruction.

The whole program

A complete MB-SDK program for our example: describe the tensors, compose library modules, write the artifacts.

 1MM, DDR2GM, GM2DDR = load_module("MM"), load_module("DDR2GM"), load_module("GM2DDR")
 2M, K, N = 64, 4096, 256
 3
 4def build(args):
 5    torch.manual_seed(0)
 6    B = torch.randn(K, N)
 7    rc = ResourceConfig(gangs=args.gangs)
 8    phase = Phase("compute", memory_manager=MemoryManager(), enable_all_sync=True)1
 9    with phase.create_context():
10        A = DDRTensor("input", shape=[M, K], tensor_type=DDRTensorType.INPUT,2
11                      num_format=NumFormat.BFP16_64, torch_data_type=torch.float32)
12        C = DDRTensor("output", shape=[M, N], tensor_type=DDRTensorType.OUTPUT,
13                      num_format=NumFormat.FP16, torch_data_type=torch.float16)
14        mm = MM("MM", resource_config=rc, m=M, k=K, n=N)3
15        mm.load_state_dict({"weight": B})  # B goes to the stash once, at load
16        A_gm = A.to_gm(placement_spec=mm.get_gm_placement("input"))
17        C_gm = C.to_gm(placement_spec=mm.get_gm_placement("output"))
18        DDR2GM("A_in", resource_config=rc).compose(A, A_gm)
19        mm.compose(A_gm, C_gm)
20        GM2DDR("C_out", resource_config=rc).compose(C_gm, C)
21    generate_artifacts({}, args.output_dir, [phase], phase.memory_manager)4

matmul_main.py, the part that builds the program. Imports: torch, sdk (Phase, MemoryManager, ResourceConfig, DDRTensor, NumFormat, generate_artifacts) and library.registry. The whole file is in the backup.

1Phase

Collects every gang's instructions and the tensors they use.

2Tensors

A in DDR as BFP16, C out as FP16. to_gm puts each where the module wants it.

3Modules

MM, DDR2GM, GM2DDR from the library. compose emits each gang's instructions.

4Artifacts

Writes the files the card runs.

This is the whole program, not a sketch: I'll build it on slide 24 and run it on a card a few slides later. The gangs come from the command line, so the same file builds for two gangs or four.

A, C and the module are all there is to it. MM decides where A, B and C live in GM and the stash; the library's DDR2GM and GM2DDR modules move A in and C out.

Inside a module: one kernel per gang

Slide 22's DDR2GM, written out: a Kernel is one gang's instructions; a Module builds one per gang.

1Kernel the instructions of one gang

 1class LoadKernel(IOKernel):  # a Kernel: the instructions of one gang
 2    @classmethod
 3    def _interface_spec(cls):
 4        return (TensorSpec("src", placement="ddr", direction="input"),
 5                TensorSpec("dst", placement="gm", direction="output"))
 6    def _build(self, src, dst, **kwargs):  # dst: this gang's view of the GM tensor
 7        for move in src.get_ddr2gm_instructions(dst, self.gang_rank):
 8            self.add_instruction(move, gang_rank=self.gang_rank,  # one MOVE_DDR2GM
 9                                 auto_data_tracking=True,
10                                 auto_resource_tracking=True)

2Module one kernel per gang, no instructions of its own

1class Load(Module):  # a Module: one kernel per gang, no instructions of its own
2    ...  # _interface_spec, _param_spec
3    def _compose(self, src, dst, **kwargs):
4        for g in self.resource_config.make_gangranks():
5            kernel = LoadKernel(f"load_{g}", g, parent=self)
6            self.add_kernel(kernel)
7            kernel.build(src, dst)

MM has the same shape

Each gang's kernel gets a view of its columns:
b.view(col_range=…, gang_rank=…)

Swap Load in for DDR2GM and every build file is byte-identical: the program that ran on a Corsair card. The full classes are in backup.

This is slide 22's DDR2GM written out. The kernel is the instructions of one gang: for each piece of this gang's view of the GM tensor, one MOVE_DDR2GM, added with automatic dependency tracking. The module emits nothing itself: it makes one kernel per gang in its ResourceConfig and builds each.

MM has the same shape with more kinds of instructions, and its module also gives each kernel a view of B's and C's columns. That is why the gang list is a flag: on four gangs, each kernel gets 64 of C's 256 columns.

Every module in the library has a main like this one, and they all share the common flags: which gangs, where to write, and whether to run and check on a card. The second command builds the same program with the library's own matmul main.

The two qjson files are the two gangs' programs, which we look at next. The dmmq ties them into one job. The weights get their own job, run once at load. The run recipe is what the debugger uses.

The graph MB-SDK records

MB-SDK records a dependency graph for each gang. Written out, it's called djson.

Gang 0 of our example, from the build. Each node is one instruction; read left to right.

  • 4 DDR2GM, one per slice. The 4 slices split K, so each slice's GM gets its quarter of A (64 × 1024).
  • 2 MATMULs, on all 8 cores. Each core multiplies its slice's quarter of K for its 64 columns. Its output buffer now holds a partial sum.
  • 4 OB2OB, the first adds. For each of the 2 cores: slice 0 adds into slice 1, and slice 2 into slice 3.
  • 2 OB2OB, the last add. Slice 1 into slice 3, one per core; it writes FP16. OB2GM and GM2DDR take C out.
grey

Added by the SDK to end the job, not part of the matmul. DE_BARRIER 2001 waits until gang 1 is done; GM2GM 2029 tells gang 1 it may finish; SEND tells the host the job is complete. More on slide 49.

The first half showed an ISA graph; this is the real one for gang 0 of our example. Each node is an instruction and each edge a dependency.

The SDK writes this graph when you pass generate_djsons=True to generate_artifacts.

From the graph to queues

Gang 0's queue runs one task group after another: in ORDER_ID order.

How a queue runs

  • A queue runs one task group at a time: a concurrent group of up to 16 tasks. Groups go in ORDER_ID order.
  • The tasks in a group run concurrently.
  • DE_BARRIER is a task too: the tasks after it wait until the tasks before it are done. It is the only order inside a group.
  • ALL_SYNC: every gang meets here at the end of the job (slide 49).
From the build. Gang 1 runs the same compute tasks; only gang 0, the leader, sends to the host. SEND is a control instruction: the gang CPU runs it.

This is gang 0's queue as the build wrote it, one task per row. ORDER_ID 1 loads A and B, moves A into the input buffers and multiplies; ORDER_ID 2 adds the slices' sums and writes C out. The tasks in a group run concurrently; each DE_BARRIER holds back the tasks after it until the tasks before it are done, because the next step needs the results of the one before.

ORDER_ID 3 is ALL_SYNC, where all the gangs meet; slide 49 looks inside it. Then SEND tells the host the job is done.

Loading the program: dmmq in, graph id out

The dmmq is the contract. Loading it turns each gang's qjson into the binary that gang runs, and gives back a graph id.

Load once, call many times: each loaded dmmq has a graph id, and every job names one.

The build wrote a dmmq: the contract for one call, with the function's signature and the program for each gang. Loading it turns each gang's qjson into the binary that gang runs and puts it on the card; what comes back is a graph id.

The weights have their own dmmq and graph id; we run that once. Every call after that is a job that names the compute graph's id.

A job: one call on one card

A job is one call of a program on one card. The host adds one row to the job queue; the gangs pick it up on their own.

Decoupled execution: nobody launches the gangs. Each gang polls the job queue on its own, starts when it sees the row, and runs at its own pace. The program reads its arguments, A's and C's addresses, from the row, so one program serves every call.

A job is one call. The program and its weights were loaded once; each call adds one row to the job queue in card memory, with the job id, the graph id of the loaded program, and its arguments: here A's and C's addresses.

Nobody launches the gangs. Each gang's CPU polls the queue, sees the new row, and starts on its own, so gangs start and finish at different times. The job is done when every gang is done, and the host gets one completion and reads C.

The host side in Python: ES Core

From your own program: open the card, load the programs once, run the weight load once, then one row per call.

 1import dmx.device as dmx_device
 2
 3dev = dmx_device.CorsairDevice(dmx_device.CorsairDeviceConfig())
 4dev.create_job_queue(entries, columns)
 5dev.register_job_callback(on_done)   # on_done(job_id, result)
 6dev.start()
 7
 8load = dev.load_graph("out/param_load_compute_c0.dmmq")  # graph ids
 9mm = dev.load_graph("out/compute_c0.dmmq")
10dev.enqueue(1, load, [])             # B into the stash, once
11
12a = dev.alloc_memory(a_size, dmx_device.Placement())
13c = dev.alloc_memory(c_size, dmx_device.Placement())
14dev.dma_write(a, a_bytes)            # A
15dev.enqueue(2, mm, [a, c])           # one call: one row
16# ... on_done(2, CallbackResult.SUCCESS)
17C = dev.dma_read(c)

Load once

Both jobs load at the start. The weight load runs once; the compute job runs per call.

One call, one row

enqueue names the program and passes the buffers for A and C.

No wait call

Your callback runs when the job's one completion arrives. Then read C.

This is the job queue from the last slide, driven from your own code with ES Core. There is no wait call: ES Core calls you back when the job's one completion arrives.

The weights went in once, as their own job. Every call after that is one row: new A, new C, same program.

The host side in C++: ES Core

The same steps in C++. The API is the same; the job queue is its own object.

 1#include "aviator_es/core/device/corsair_device.h"
 2#include "aviator_es/core/job/job_queue.h"
 3using namespace aviator_core;
 4
 5CorsairDevice device(CorsairDeviceConfig{.card = 0});
 6JobQueue jobs(device, entries, columns);
 7GraphId load = *device.LoadGraph("out/param_load_compute_c0.dmmq");
 8GraphId mm = *device.LoadGraph("out/compute_c0.dmmq");
 9device.RegisterJobCallback([&](JobId id, DeviceInterface::CallbackResult r) {
10  /* r == DeviceInterface::CallbackResult::kSuccess: job id is done */ });
11device.Start();
12
13jobs.AddJob(load, {});                                 // B into the stash, once
14DeviceBuffer a = *device.AllocMemory(a_bytes, Placement());
15DeviceBuffer c = *device.AllocMemory(c_bytes, Placement());
16device.Dma(a, HostBufferRead::Of(a_host, a_bytes));    // A
17jobs.AddJob(mm, {a, c});                               // one call: one row
18// ... the callback fires
19device.Dma(HostBufferWrite::Of(c_host, c_bytes), c);   // read C

Same steps

Open the card, load both graphs, run the weight load once, then one row per call.

Job queue

AddJob(graph id, buffers) adds the row and returns the job id.

Status everywhere

Each call returns a status or a value with one. The checks are left out here.

ES Core has the same API in C++. The job queue is an object you add jobs to; AddJob takes the graph id and the buffers, and returns the job id your callback will see.

Every call returns a status; the code here leaves the checks out to fit.

Is the answer right?

The same file builds a PyTorch reference in the same number formats. The card's output must match it byte for byte.

 4    A_data = torch.randn(M, K)
 5    generate_input_output_bin(  # writes input.bin and ref_output.bin
 6        args.output_dir, ref, [TensorDescriptor("input", NumFormat.BFP16_64, tensor=A_data)])
 7

10        ok = execute_and_or_validate(args, args.output_dir)
$ (cd out && dmdbg_mcard --script script_c0)    # on a card host: writes _0_output.bin
$ python matmul_main.py -g 0 1 -o out --validate
PASSED: the card's output matches the reference, byte for byte

One command

On a card host, --validate-dmdbg builds, runs and compares. --validate compares later, without a card.

Our run: this example on a Corsair card, November 2026. The output matched the reference byte for byte.

The reference does the same arithmetic in the same formats, so the check is exact: no tolerance. Any byte that differs is a bug, in the program or in the reference.

We ran this exact file on a card: the debugger script wrote the output, and the validate step compared it with the reference. It matched byte for byte.

How fast? Aviator Bench

A benchmark is a pytest. Aviator Bench ships with Aviator: it runs the same jobs as ES Core, checks them, then times them.

One more build step end of build() in matmul_main.py

1from sdk.artifacts import generate_executor_files
2from sdk.phase import PhaseSchedule
3    ...
4    generate_executor_files(PhaseSchedule(phase), args.output_dir)

It writes executor.config how to run the program

1{"config": {"0": [
2  {"run_once": ["param_load_compute_c0.dmmq"]},             B into the stash, once
3  {"name": "compute", "stage": 0, "dmmq": ["compute_c0.dmmq"]}]}}   one job per call

Same jobs

Run once: the weight-load graph. Then each call is one job of the compute graph, as on slide 28.

Two fixtures

aviator_artifact is the build; aviator_runner owns the card.

One measurement per run

Latency or throughput: each is its own run.

Benchmarking is a pytest. Aviator Bench ships with Aviator, next to ES Core and MB-SDK, and runs the same jobs ES Core does: it checks the answer, then times it.

It needs one more file from the build: executor.config, which says to run the weight load once and then one compute job per call. One extra call in the main writes it.

The benchmark is a pytest

Check, then time. A broken run fails the test; a noisy one is recorded, not failed.

 1import bench, torch
 2from bench.qualification import evaluate_latency
 3
 4def test_matmul(aviator_artifact, aviator_runner):       # fixtures from Bench's plugin
 5    out = aviator_artifact.path                           # the build directory
 6    (stage,) = aviator_artifact.stage_ids                 # the weight load already ran
 7    a = torch.frombuffer(bytearray((out / "input.bin").read_bytes()), dtype=torch.uint8)
 8    call = bench.Call(stage=stage, inputs_by_rank={0: {"input": a.reshape(1, -1)}})
 9
10    c = aviator_runner.run(call).outputs_by_rank[0]["output"]             # one job
11    assert c.numpy().tobytes() == (out / "ref_output.bin").read_bytes()   # byte for byte
12
13    m = bench.measure(aviator_runner, work=call, mode=bench.Latency())    # fixed policy
14    assert evaluate_latency(m, expected_world_size=1).plumbing_passed     # broken fails
15    print(m.status, m.evidence_path)                      # noisy is recorded

Condensed from test_matmul_bench.py, which also checks the input's and the output's type and shape.

Check first

C must match ref_output.bin byte for byte before anything is timed.

A fixed policy

Warm-up, then three timed trials whose medians must agree, then device time for each gang.

A broken run fails; a noisy one doesn't

Broken: the timing run is incomplete, for example samples are missing, so evaluate_latency fails the test. Noisy: the three trials disagree. Bench marks the result unstable in its evidence file, and the test still passes.

Two fixtures from Bench's plugin: the artifact, which is our build directory, and the runner, which owns the card. The weight load has already run.

First one call, untimed: C must match the reference byte for byte. Then the same call under Bench's fixed latency policy. The test fails if the run is broken; if the trials disagree, that's recorded in the evidence instead of failing the test.

Run it, read the evidence

Bench's launcher runs the test on the card and writes every measurement to a JSON file.

$ python matmul_main.py -g 0 1 -o out
$ S=$(python -c 'import bench, pathlib; print(pathlib.Path(bench.__file__).parent)')
$ python -m bench.testing.mpi_pytest_main "$S/testing/mpi_pytest_child.py" 1 \
      test_matmul_bench.py --aviator-bench-artifact=out --aviator-bench-disable-recovery
[bench] correctness=PASS: C matches ref_output.bin byte for byte
[bench] host trial=0 calls=… median_us=…

What the evidence keeps

Every call's host time, the medians, device cycles per gang and trial, the policy, and which build ran.

Host time is not device time

Host time includes writing A and reading C. Device time is each gang's job time, in cycles.

See every call

--aviator-bench-trace=DIR also writes a trace of every call.

Our run: this test passed byte for byte on a Corsair card, November 2026. Measured values are left out here.

One build, one launch. The first line Bench prints is the correctness check; then the host time per trial, the device time per gang, and where the evidence went.

We ran exactly this on a Corsair card: C matched the reference byte for byte. The numbers are left off the slide; the JSON file keeps every call.

In the debugger's names, MCM is a package and soc a chiplet. The commands ran from a script; prompts added, paths shortened. Hung or slow: next slide.

Build with a debug manifest: it maps every task group back to the kernel that emitted it. list_kernels shows the kernels; break_kernel sets a stop after MM's last task group, on both gangs, because MM runs on both. Then run, read C's first tile from gang 0's GM, and continue.

In this small program the kernel's last task group is also the program's last before ALL_SYNC, so C is already computed at the stop; neither gang needs the other before ALL_SYNC, so nothing waits. The bank to read comes from phase.gm_dump() or the build's tensor metadata. After continue, the output file is _2_output.bin: compare it with cmp. On the card, the tile read at the stop matched the PyTorch reference, and the whole output matched byte for byte.

Hung or slow

The same debugger, three keys in load_c0.yaml: a timeout for a hang; counters and timestamps for speed.

Settings from the MB-SDK docs

1pcie:              # in load_c0.yaml
2  timeout:
3    enable: True
4    value: "120"     # seconds
5  perf:
6    enable: true     # counters per task group
7    counter: 3       # required with perf
8  profiling:
9    enable: true     # job timestamps per gang

Hung

  • The timeout brings the run back; it prints Graph Execution Unsuccessful.
  • Bisect with break_kernel: a stop that never comes means the hang is earlier.
  • At a stop, partner gangs wait at their DE_BARRIER: continue before the card's timeout recovery fires.
  • Recover with close 0 and open 0; reset the card only if it stays stuck.

Slow

  • perf: counters per task group. profiling: job timestamps per gang.
  • Read them in the d-Matrix Profiler: kernels and instructions per gang, slice and core.
  • Not while stops are set. Measure three runs; report cold and warm runs apart.
Before a card: artifact generation checks each gang's program against hardware limits, and the write-after-read sanitizer checks the built program.
From the MB-SDK documentation: the d-Matrix Debugger, the d-Matrix Profiler, and the kernel playbook.

For a hang, set a timeout so the run comes back instead of waiting forever; the message is quoted from the debugger, we did not hang a shared card to capture it. Then bisect with break_kernel. A stopped gang's partners wait at their DE_BARRIER, so continue promptly. Close and reopen the card; reset it only if it stays stuck.

For speed: perf counters per task group and profiling timestamps per job, read in the profiler. Neither runs while breakpoints are set. Create an output directory before turning on perf: without it, the weight-load step crashed in our run.

Attention: what it computes

Each token's output is a weighted average of the values; the weights say how well its query matches each key.

Q, K and V come from the tokens

Matmuls earlier in the layer turn each token into a query, a key and a value. Attention itself has no weights.

A causal mask

In a decoder a token may not see later tokens: scores above the diagonal become −∞ before the softmax.

Prefill and decode

Prefill runs the whole prompt at once. Decode runs one new token against the keys and values kept from earlier tokens: the KV cache.

Scaled dot-product attention. Every token makes a query, a key and a value. A token's output is a weighted average of all the values, weighted by how well its query matches each key: a dot product, scaled by one over the square root of the head dimension, then a softmax so the weights are positive and add to one. Two matmuls do almost all the arithmetic; the softmax in between is a row-wise vector operation.

The scale keeps the scores at unit size whatever the head dimension, so the softmax does not saturate. If asked for numbers: with keys [1,0], [0,1], [1,1], values [1,0], [0,2], [3,3] and the query [1,0], the weights are 0.401, 0.198, 0.401 and the output is [1.604, 1.599].

Attention is three library modules

SDPAPrefill composes QKTPrefill, Softmax and XVPrefill: two matmuls on the DIMCs, a softmax on the SIMD engines.

1sdpa = SDPAPrefill(name="sdpa", resource_config=rc, pt_model=ref,
2                   d_head=64, max_q_prompt_len=64, query_tile_size=64, max_seq_len=64, ...)
3sdpa.compose(Q_gm, K_gm, V_gm, k_cache, v_cache, O_gm)   # one module, like mm.compose
4
5# inside SDPAPrefill._compose, for each head and query tile:
6self.qkt_modules[idx].compose(curr_query, k_cache_tens, curr_attention_scores, ...)
7self.softmax_modules[idx].compose(curr_attention_scores, curr_softmax_output, ...)
8self.xv_modules[idx].compose(xv_input, v_cache_tens, curr_xv_output, value_tens, ...)
Condensed from sdpa_prefill_main.py and sdpa_prefill.py; the real loop also handles heads, masks and several gangs.

The program side looks like our matmul: build one module and compose it. Inside, SDPAPrefill composes three library modules per head and per query tile: QKTPrefill computes the scores, Softmax scales them, applies the causal mask if there is one, and normalizes each row, and XVPrefill multiplies by V. The customer MB-SDK docs describe the module the same way.

Decode is the same shape with QKTDecode, Softmax and XVDecode, for one new token. An optional fused path folds the softmax into the first matmul; the docs keep the unfused path as the default.

What one gang runs

The same paths as our matmul: Q and P travel like A, Kᵀ and V like B.

A's path: GM → input buffer

Q for the first matmul, then P, the softmax output, for the second.

B's path: stash → weight buffer

Kᵀ, then V. Prefill leaves both in the stash: the KV cache that each decode step reads.

One gang, d_head 64, 64 tokens: 32 instructions, 2 of them MATMUL and 1 EXEC_SIMD. Ran on a Corsair card; matched the reference byte for byte.

This is the smallest configuration, the one the nightly tests run: one gang, one 64 by 64 tile. Q, K and V come into GM. The data rearrangement engine transposes K on its way into the stash, where it becomes the K cache. The first matmul takes Q through the input buffer and K-transpose through the weight buffer, exactly where A and B went in our matmul. The scores go to the SIMD engine for the softmax, and the second matmul takes the probabilities as A and V as B.

Thirty-two instructions in all: two matmuls, one SIMD call, a transpose, and moves and barriers. We built it with sdpa_prefill_main.py in about a minute, ran it on a Corsair card, and the output matched the PyTorch reference byte for byte.

Number formats in our matmul

The DIMCs compute in block floating point; results leave as FP16.

FormatUsed forWhat it is
BFP16_64A: DDR, GM, input buffer8-bit values; each row block of 64 shares one 8-bit exponent
BFP16_64_COLB: stash, weight bufferThe same, with blocks down a column
BFP12_128_COLSmaller weights4-bit values; column blocks of 128
SBFP12Compressed weights in the stash4-bit values; 16 down a column share an 8-bit scale. Expanded to BFP16 on the way to the weight buffer (backup)
BFP32_1Sums in the output bufferWide partial sums: a 24-bit value and an 8-bit exponent each
FP16C, and the SIMD engineThe last add writes FP16
Formats change on the moves: data is converted as it moves between memories, not by a separate instruction.
The first half's MXINT8 is MB-SDK's BFP16_64: 8-bit values, one exponent per 64. (The OCP MX spec's MXINT8 uses blocks of 32.)

In our matmul: A arrives as BFP16 blocked along rows; B sits in the stash as BFP16 blocked down columns. Sums stay wide in the output buffers, and the last add writes FP16, which is what comes back to the host. SBFP12 is the compressed weight format; a backup slide shows its layout.

Block floating point, block by block

A block of values shares one exponent; each value keeps a small signed integer. A 64 × 64 tile is stored as 65 rows.

The largest value in a block sets its exponent, so small values lose their low bits. Fewer bits per value, as in BFP12, lose more.

Block floating point: every value in a block shares one exponent, and each value keeps only a small signed integer. Activations block along rows, weights down columns, so a 64 by 64 tile is 64 rows of 8-bit values plus one row of exponents: 65 rows.

On one block through the SDK's quantizer, with 12.5 the largest value, the step is 0.125: 12.5, 3.0 and 0.75 come back exactly, -0.3 comes back as -0.25, and 0.04 and 0.004 become 0. BFP12 keeps 4 bits per value and loses more, in exchange for half the memory.

An activation on the SIMD engine

Each core has a SIMD engine beside its output buffer. One EXEC_SIMD runs GeLU where the sums already are.

From our build: matmul + GeLU

One EXEC_SIMD on both cores of the slice that holds the final sums, then OB2GM sends the result. One instruction more than the plain matmul.

The library's SIMD kernels

Activations (GeLU, SiLU, ReLU, SwiGLU), element-wise math, and reductions.

The SIMD engine does the math the DIMCs don't. Fusing GeLU here costs one instruction and no trip through GM.

More queues: streams and events

One stream is one queue. An event lets one queue wait for another.

 1s0 = phase.create_stream("mm_slice_0")
 2s1 = phase.create_stream("mm_slice_1")
 3s2 = phase.create_stream("mm_slice_2")
 4e1 = phase.create_event("stream_1_done")
 5e2 = phase.create_event("stream_2_done")
 6with s1:
 7    mm[1].compose(a[1], c[1]); e1.signal(...)
 8with s2:
 9    mm[2].compose(a[2], c[2]); e2.signal(...)
10with s0:
11    mm[0].compose(a[0], c[0])
12    e1.wait(...); e2.wait(...)
13    GM2DDR(...).compose(c, c_ddr)  # all of C

The three queues, from the build

queue 1 · s0
loadsMATMULOB2GMwait e1wait e2GM2DDR×3
queue 2 · s1
loadsMATMULOB2GMsignal e1
queue 3 · s2
loadsMATMULOB2GMsignal e2

loads = DDR2GM, ST2WB, GM2IB. A signal and a wait are each a DE_BARRIER. Up to 8 streams per gang.

From the build: three 64 × 512 × 64 matmuls on one gang, one per queue.

By default everything goes on one queue. Open streams and independent work runs on separate queues at the same time; here, three matmuls.

An event joins them: one queue's DE_BARRIER signals it, another queue's DE_BARRIER waits for it. Queue 1 writes all of C only after the other two have signalled.

EXEC_CPU: the gang CPU as a functional unit

EXEC_CPU runs a function on the gang CPU as one more task in the dataflow graph.

Data-dependent moves

Which rows or tokens to move depends on values computed earlier: embedding lookup, MoE token grouping and ungrouping.

Waiting on the outside

Poll a flag that a GPU or the host writes, then let the graph go on (slides 52, 54).

Control and coordination

Decisions and bookkeeping that suit a general-purpose core better than the matrix or vector units.

The heavy math stays on the DIMCs and SIMD engines. While a function runs, only its own queue waits.

Each gang has a RISC-V CPU next to its dispatch engine. EXEC_CPU puts a function on that CPU into the dataflow graph as one more task: it waits on its inputs like a MOVE or a MATMUL, and the tasks after it wait on it. So the CPU is a functional unit of the graph, alongside the DMA, the DIMCs and the SIMD engines.

What the library uses it for today: data-dependent moves, such as embedding lookup and MoE token grouping, where the function works out which rows go where and issues the moves; and waiting for a flag that a GPU or the host writes, as in the low-latency loop on slide 54. While a function runs, only the queue that called it waits; the other queues keep going.

Fewer instructions for the same work

One instruction can address many units. Chiplet is an index; gang, slice and core are bit masks.

1Command multicast: one instruction, many cores

instructionscore ops
MATMUL216
GM2IB216
ST2WB416
total848

One MATMUL drives all 64 DIMCs of the gang: 4 slices × 2 cores, 8 DIMCs each. Per gang, in our build: 8 instructions do 48 core operations.

2Repeat modifier (RepMod)

An instruction can carry only the fields that change from the previous one on the same unit.

The ISA supports it; MB-SDK support is in progress.

Hot Chips 2025 called the first one command multicast.

One MATMUL addressed to all four slices and both cores drives 64 DIMCs, so gang 0's whole matmul needs eight such instructions. The repeat modifier goes further: a follower sends only what changed.

Multicast support: one MOVE, many gangs

Data multicast: a MOVE can name a chiplet and a mask of its gangs, and one transfer lands in all of them.

Useful when

Several gangs need the same data: a layer's output that every gang's slice of the next matmul reads, a replicated weight, or a reduced result sent back to all.
The receivers share a chiplet: one MOVE covers up to its 4 gangs. A whole package takes one per chiplet: 4 MOVEs instead of 15.
It can land at the same GM address on each receiver: place the receiving tensor alike on every gang. The library's broadcast does this.
Sending is on the critical path: small transfers to many gangs, where one MOVE per gang would add up.
Not for different data per gang: that is still one MOVE per gang.

Data multicast. Slide 45 sent one instruction to many units; here one MOVE_GM2GM names a destination chiplet and a mask of its gangs, and the same bytes land at the same GM address in every gang it names.

Each receiver still waits with its own DE_BARRIER; Communication (slide 49) covers that pairing. A broadcast from one gang to its whole package is one MOVE per chiplet: three to the other chiplets and one to the other three gangs of its own chiplet. The library's broadcast kernels choose these MOVEs.

Fields filled in at run time

Where an instruction reads or writes, how much it moves and how often it loops can change at run time. The operation itself is fixed when you build.

WhenIn MB-SDKExample
Build or loada constantweight addresses
Each calljobqueue(i)this call's buffers, the next KV write position
Each iterationloopA() inside phase.loop(n)the next iteration's window
A conditionphase.execute_if(c)a block that runs 0 or 1 times
From dataload(addr), or EXEC_CPUhow many tokens each expert got
1relu_on = Scalar("relu_on", default_value=args.relu_on)  # a field in each job's row
2with phase.execute_if(jobqueue(relu_on.jq_id) >= 1):  # runs 0 or 1 times, per call
3    relu.compose(C_gm, C_gm)                          # in place, in GM
4
5rows = {"row_offset": loopA() * M, "max_offset": (ROUNDS - 1) * M}
6with phase.loop(ROUNDS, split_streams=False):  # one LOOP_A per gang, ROUNDS times
7    DDRWindowLoad("A_in", resource_config=rc).compose(A, A_gm, **rows)

When fields are filled

Before the job starts, from the row. Fields that use a loop counter are refilled each iteration.

The box is from two programs that ran on a Corsair card and matched their references byte for byte: relu_if, with the field at 1 and at 0, and mm_loop, four 64-row windows.

The first half showed why fields change: context length and expert choice change every step. Here is how you write it in MB-SDK.

The box is real code. relu_if declares relu_on, a field in each job's row, and runs the ReLU only when the call sets it to 1; for both values the program is the same, byte for byte, and only the row differs. mm_loop runs slide 22's matmul over four 64-row windows of a taller A; the loop index sets the DDR addresses. For data-dependent work beyond these, the program calls EXEC_CPU (slide 44).

Example: one decode step

The job's row carries the prompt length and the token index. Where this token's K and V go, and its RoPE position, are expressions on them.

1from sdk.dynamic_expr import jobqueue
2prompt = jobqueue(prompt_len_col)
3token = jobqueue(token_iter_col)
4aligned = (prompt + 63) // 64 * 64
5row = aligned + (token - prompt)  # K, V go here
6position = jobqueue(token_iter_col)  # RoPE

The gang fills these in from the row before the job starts. Nothing is recompiled per token.

One program serves every decode step. Only the row changes.

This is the row from slide 28, with two more fields. The library's KV-cache and rotary kernels read them, so the write position and the rotation follow the token without the host touching the program.

Call it the token's position, or its row in the cache.

A MOVE into the other gang, a DE_BARRIER on the receiver

The sender's MOVE carries a task id; the receiver's DE_BARRIER waits for it. A gather of your own:

 1class Gather(Collective):
 2    @classmethod
 3    def _interface_spec(cls):
 4        return (TensorSpec("shards", placement="gm", direction="input"),
 5                TensorSpec("full", placement="gm", direction="output"))
 6    def _build(self, shards, full, **kwargs):
 7        gangs = self.resource_config.make_gangranks()
 8        root, sends = gangs[0], {}
 9        for g in gangs:
10            mine = {tile: tile for tile in shards.coords_for_gang_rank(g)}
11            moves = shards.get_gm2gm_transfers(full, g, dst_gang_rank=root,
12                                               src_coord_to_dst_coord=mine)
13            for move in moves:  # a MOVE_GM2GM issued by gang g, into the root's GM
14                self.add_instruction(move, gang_rank=g, auto_data_tracking=True,
15                                     auto_resource_tracking=True)
16            if g != root:
17                sends[g] = moves
18        # Each cross-gang MOVE gets a task id; the root, a DE_BARRIER waiting on it.
19        barriers = resolve_intergang_receives(self.phase, sends,
20                                              fuse_send_recv=False)
21        for barrier in barriers.get(root, []):
22            self.add_instruction(barrier, gang_rank=root, auto_data_tracking=True)

What it builds 2 gangs

ALL_SYNC is built the same way

Gang 1's MOVE_GM2GM 2001, gang 0's DE_BARRIER 2001, then back with 2029: task ids the SDK keeps for its own sync.

The sender's completion means sent, not landed. Only the receiver's barrier proves arrival.
No receive call: the MOVE carries the task id. Ran on a Corsair card; C matched the reference byte for byte.

A Collective is the SDK class for code that crosses gangs, next to Kernel and Module. This one gathers C: each gang MOVEs its columns into gang 0's GM. resolve_intergang_receives gives each cross-gang MOVE a task id and the receiver a DE_BARRIER on it, so gang 0 waits for exactly the MOVEs it needs. On four gangs, gang 0 runs three receive barriers.

ALL_SYNC, at the end of every job, is built from the same two instructions: 2001 and 2029 are task ids the SDK reserves for its own sync. Multicast, one MOVE to many gangs, was on slide 46.

MOVE_xx2PCI to another package, card or node

The same pattern reaches other packages and cards: the MOVE writes into the other side's memory over PCIe, and the receiving gang's DE_BARRIER waits on the task id.

JetStream

Our transparent NIC carries PCIe semantics over Ethernet. Product pipelines run within one node today.

The sender knows the address because placement is fixed at build time, or because the host set up the buffer once and passed its address in the job row.

Collectives such as ALL_SYNC are built from these MOVEs and barriers inside the program.

Many cards from the host: one MPI rank per card

On the host, MPI is real: one rank drives one card. Activations go card to card as MOVEs, with no host in the data path.

1Ranks

One MPI process per card. Rank 0 leads.

2Load

Each rank loads its card's part of the model.

3Run

The leader sends the command and inputs; every rank runs its card's job.

4Activations

A MOVE_DDR2PCI into the next card's DDR; a DE_BARRIER there waits on it.

5Results

Workers send outputs to the leader.

Each rank sets world_size, rank_to_card and local_rank in its ES Core CorsairDeviceConfig.

Inside a card, gangs act like MPI ranks. On the host it isn't an analogy: ES Dist runs one MPI process per card, and rank 0 leads.

Control goes over MPI: commands, inputs and results. Activations don't: a pipeline stage's last gangs MOVE them straight into the next card's DDR, and a DE_BARRIER on the next card waits for them.

GPU and Corsair: stores and a flag

The GPU kernel writes data directly into Corsair memory, and neither side waits on a host CPU. (d-Matrix, Oct 12 2026)

If you know NVSHMEM put-with-signal, this has the same shape, without a symmetric heap: each side writes into buffers the other set up once.

A GPU store can't release a DE barrier, so a short function on the gang CPU watches the flag.

Pairing a GPU with Corsair

Attention-FFN disaggregation pairs them once per layer. Speculative decoding pairs them once per draft round.

Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD)

8 Corsair cards run all experts as one Corsair graph; two root cards relay to the other six. Each layer is one round trip: 24 layers plus the LM head. Hidden 2880; top-4 of 32 experts.

845 tokens/s per userGPT-OSS-20B · one H100 + 8 Corsair cards(d-Matrix, Oct 12 2026)

Speculative decoding

  • Draft on Corsair, verify on the GPU.
  • Today the two hosts exchange token ids over TCP. Inside the drafter, the cards pass activations to each other on their own.
  • The stores-and-flag path of AFD applies here too.
  • Joint work with Gimlet Labs.

Decode reads every weight once per token. The matmuls over fixed weights run on the cards, where the weights stay in on-chip memory; the GPU keeps attention over the growing KV cache.

Low-latency inference: keep the program on the card

For a small model called in a tight loop, the call costs more than the compute. Keep one job running on the card and feed it directly.

One job per callwrite a row→gangs poll→run→ALL_SYNC→completion
Resident loopwrite the input→run one pass→write the output

No job submitted per call. No DMA started by the host. GM direct write is experimental in ES Core.

Science uses: feedback control, event triggers, a surrogate called every timestep.

The resident loop applies on-device control to a single small model: the host writes straight into one GM bank and polls one page for the answer.

Backup

Aviator: Performant Matmul Lowering

  • Performance by sustained DIMC active operation:
    • Pipelined, overlapped computation + communication (ping-pong buffering)
    • Minimized data path overhead (data multicast, strided transfers)
    • Instruction merging to exploit symmetric patterns (command multicast)

Aviator: Inference Engine for LLM Serving

  • Brain of serving infra
  • Tensor and Pipeline Parallelism (TP and PP)
  • Model-aware algos
  • Dynamic cache mgt
  • Advanced features (Paged Attention, Continuous Batching, Speculative Decoding)
  • One per card – thin, largely asynchronous
  • Continuous, async request queue
  • Minimal worker IPC – none on critical path
  • Minimal H2D, D2H interaction
Distributed, high perf, multi-modal capable inference serving stack

32        mm.load_state_dict({"weight": B})  # B goes to the stash once, at load
33        A_gm = A.to_gm(placement_spec=mm.get_gm_placement("input"))
34        C_gm = C.to_gm(placement_spec=mm.get_gm_placement("output"))
35        DDR2GM("A_in", resource_config=rc).compose(A, A_gm)
36        mm.compose(A_gm, C_gm)
37        GM2DDR("C_out", resource_config=rc).compose(C_gm, C)

own_load_main.py: what changes

 1class LoadKernel(IOKernel):  # a Kernel: the instructions of one gang
 2    @classmethod
 3    def _interface_spec(cls):
 4        return (TensorSpec("src", placement="ddr", direction="input"),
 5                TensorSpec("dst", placement="gm", direction="output"))
 6    def _build(self, src, dst, **kwargs):  # dst: this gang's view of the GM tensor
 7        for move in src.get_ddr2gm_instructions(dst, self.gang_rank):
 8            self.add_instruction(move, gang_rank=self.gang_rank,  # one MOVE_DDR2GM
 9                                 auto_data_tracking=True,
10                                 auto_resource_tracking=True)
11class Load(Module):  # a Module: one kernel per gang, no instructions of its own
12    @classmethod
13    def _interface_spec(cls):
14        return LoadKernel.interface_spec()
15    @classmethod
16    def _param_spec(cls):
17        return ()
18    def _compose(self, src, dst, **kwargs):
19        for g in self.resource_config.make_gangranks():
20            kernel = LoadKernel(f"load_{g}", g, parent=self)
21            self.add_kernel(kernel)
22            kernel.build(src, dst)

Row-sharded matmul: split K, exchange partial sums

Splitting K adds one exchange: per gang, two MOVE_OB2OB out and two DE_BARRIERs in.

In MB-SDK

MMKSharded(..., collective="reduce-scatter")

In MPI terms, a reduce-scatter. It's a library module.

Cost

Gang 0 runs 67 instructions instead of 25. Most of the extra ones re-tile the partial sums through GM before the exchange.

When to split K

K is large, N is narrow, or the input already arrives split along K.

Split K and each gang ends with a partial sum of all of C, so the partials must be added. Each gang writes the rows the other owns straight into that gang's output buffer, then waits for its own half on the matching task ids.

The SDK also runs a short sync between the two gangs before the exchange.

Wrong weights or wrong math? Look between jobs

No stops needed: run the weight-load job and the compute job one at a time, and read memory in between.

Commands customer-documented

(dmdbg) open 0
(dmdbg) load 0 load_c0.yaml
(dmdbg) execute 0 run_param_load_compute_c0.yaml   # B into the stash
(dmdbg) read mem 0 0 l soc0.gang0.slice0.stash0.stbank0 4160
(dmdbg) execute 0 run_compute_c0.yaml               # one call
(dmdbg) read mem 0 0 l soc0.gang0.slice0.gm.bank2 8192

What it printed on a Corsair card, trimmed

Graph Execution Successful
DMA Read Status:  0
Data Saved in soc0.gang0.slice0.stash0.stbank0.bin
Saving Output
Graph Execution Successful
Data Saved in soc0.gang0.slice0.gm.bank2.bin

The stash

4,160 bytes: B's first BFP16 tile, 65 rows of 64 bytes, byte for byte as the SDK wrote it.

GM

C's first tile equals the PyTorch reference.

The output

Matches the reference byte for byte.

Two reads separate a data problem from a compute problem.

Without breakpoints: load, execute the weight-load job, read the stash, execute one call, read GM. If the stash bytes are wrong, the weights or their conversion are wrong; if they are right and GM is wrong, the math is. In our run both were right.

Compose two modules: MM, then ReLU

 1class MatmulRelu(Module):
 2    def __init__(self, name, *, resource_config, m, k, n):
 3        super().__init__(name, resource_config=resource_config, m=m, k=k, n=n)
 4        self.mm = MM("mm", resource_config=resource_config, m=m, k=k, n=n,
 5                     parent=self)
 6        self.relu = SIMD("relu", resource_config=resource_config, m=m, n=n,
 7                         simd_operator="relu", parent=self)
 8    @classmethod
 9    def _interface_spec(cls):  # the ports: A in, C out, both in GM
10        return (TensorSpec("input", placement="gm", direction="input"),
11                TensorSpec("output", placement="gm", direction="output"))
12    @classmethod
13    def _param_spec(cls):  # no weight of its own: B belongs to self.mm
14        return ()
15    def _get_gm_placement(self, tensor):  # A as MM reads it, C as ReLU writes it
16        child = self.mm if tensor == "input" else self.relu
17        return child.get_gm_placement(tensor)
18    def _compose(self, a, c, **kwargs):
19        tmp = GMTensor("tmp", [self.mm.m, self.mm.n], num_format=NumFormat.FP16,
20                       placement_spec=self.relu.get_gm_placement("input"))
21        self.mm.compose(a, tmp)    # A x B -> tmp, in GM
22        self.relu.compose(tmp, c)  # relu(tmp) -> C, on the SIMD engines
23...  # in build(), inside the phase context:
24mmr = MatmulRelu("MMRelu", resource_config=rc, m=M, k=K, n=N)
25mmr.load_state_dict({"mm.weight": B},  # to the child self.mm; B goes to
26                    instruction_graph="param_load")  # the stash once, at load

Weights load once

instruction_graph="param_load": without it, the child's weights reload on every call.

What composing costs

2 gangs: 29 / 28 instructions per gang against 25 / 24 for slide 22's matmul. Through GM: +2 GM2OB, +1 EXEC_SIMD, +2 OB2GM, one GM2DDR fewer. Fused, MM(..., add_simd_kernel="relu"): +1 (built only).

Checked

Ran on a Corsair card: byte for byte against relu(A × B).

A module can be built from modules: _compose wires MM into the library's SIMD ReLU through a GM tensor. The parent passes its weights to the child with load_state_dict; pass instruction_graph="param_load" so they load once, not on every call.

Halo exchange with RowCopy

A halo exchange in library code: sync, then copy each edge row into the neighbour's halo.

 1def halo_map(n_gangs):
 2    pairs = []
 3    for g in range(n_gangs - 1):  # gangs g and g+1 swap their edge rows
 4        pairs.append((g * S + HG, (g + 1) * S))          # down, into g+1's top halo
 5        pairs.append(((g + 1) * S + 1, g * S + HG + 1))  # up, into g's bottom halo
 6    return pairs
 7...  # in build(), inside the phase context:
 8    strip_of_row = {(r, 0): [GMBankLoc(*gangs[r // S].to_tuple(), slice=0, bank=0)]
 9                    for r in range(len(gangs) * S)}  # strip g lives on gang g
10    x = X.to_gm(coords_to_banks=strip_of_row, tile_max_height=1)  # one row per tile
11    DDR2GM("x_in", resource_config=rc).compose(X, x)
12    phase.sync_gangs(rc)  # every gang has loaded its strip before any copy starts
13    halo = RowCopy("halo", resource_config=rc, row_map=halo_map(len(gangs)), cols=W)
14    halo.build(x, x)  # each copy: a MOVE into the neighbour's GM, a DE_BARRIER there
15    GM2DDR("x_out", resource_config=rc).compose(x, Y)

The grid

[gangs × 8, 64] FP16, split by rows. Strip g is a top halo row, 6 rows and a bottom halo row.

Each copy

A MOVE into the neighbour's GM and a DE_BARRIER there. sync_gangs first: every strip is loaded before any copy.

Checked

Ran on a Corsair card on 2 and 4 gangs: byte for byte.

RowCopy is the library's row-copy kernel: one MOVE and one receive barrier per copy. Without the sync, one run came back with 3 of 6 halo rows still holding their loaded values: consistent with a race between a gang's own load of a halo row and the neighbour's MOVE into it, not proven. The write-after-read sanitizer does not flag it: these are two writes.

SBFP12: compressed weights, expanded on the move

SBFP12 keeps a 64 × 64 weight tile in 37 rows instead of 65; the move into the weight buffer expands it back to BFP16.

In MB-SDK, set MM's weight format to NumFormat.SBFP12. MM works out E_BIAS, one per tensor, from the weights; MOVE_ST2WB uses it to expand each tile.
The stash holds about 1.7× as many weights in SBFP12 as in BFP16.

SBFP12 is the stash format for compressed weights. Each column of a 64 by 64 tile is cut into four blocks of 16 values. Each value is 4 bits, each block has an 8-bit scale (4 exponent bits, 4 mantissa bits), and each column has one exponent: 37 rows of 64 bytes instead of 65.

MOVE_ST2WB expands each tile to BFP16 in the weight buffer as it moves, using one exponent bias for the whole tensor, so the matmul itself is unchanged. MM computes that bias when it loads the weights.
